report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Phantom limb sensations persist in most amputees and offer a window into how the body is represented without sensory input from the missing limb.
In this state, vision may help resolve conflicts between the perceived body and the physical world.
In obstacle tolerance (OBT), the phantom remains present despite overlapping with physical matter; in obstacle shunning (OBS), it retracts or disappears.
Whether these experiences extend beyond subjective perception to visual attention during action remains unclear.
We tested whether OBS and OBT are associated with distinct gaze and taskperformance patterns during obstacle avoidance.
Fifteen individuals with transradial amputation (7 OBS, 8 OBT) and 29 able-bodied controls physically executed or imagined a limb repositioning movement while avoiding an obstacle.
We recorded gaze using mobile eye-tracking and quantified obstacle-directed dwell time using automated obstacle segmentation and fixation detection.
We analysed trial duration and attention shifts between the obstacle and the limb or environment.
Bayesian mixed-effects models showed that participants with OBT spent less time looking at the obstacle when using the affected rather than the intact limb during motor execution.
They were also more likely to make three or fewer attention shifts with the affected-limb, suggesting reduced obstacle monitoring when phantom-object overlap is tolerated.
Participants with OBS took longer than controls during both motor execution and motor imagery.
These findings suggest that OBS and OBT are associated with distinct action-related visuospatial strategies.
Phantom-object relations appear to extend beyond subjective experience to the visual and temporal organisation of behaviour around physical objects.
• Phantom retraction near obstacles was linked to longer trial durations.
• Phantom-object tolerance was linked to reduced obstacle-directed gaze and fewer attention shifts during affected-limb movements.
• Gaze dynamics and task timing indexed phantom-object representation during action.

While the body is the primary instrument with which we perceive the world around us, it also provides the reference frame through which external space is structured and action is controlled (Bermúdez, 1998; Blanke, 2012; Gallagher, 2003).

text.text: Limb amputation disrupts this reference frame, yet the missing limb often remains present in phenomenological experience.

Many persons with an amputation report phantom limb sensations (PLS), including postural, motor, tactile, thermal and/or painful qualities of the absent limb (Giummarra et al., 2007 (Giummarra et al., , 2010;; V. Ramachandran & Hirstein, 1998).

text.text: These sensations vary markedly across individuals and over time, indicating that body representation remains plastic after the loss of the physical limb.

Current accounts suggest that phantom limb experiences emerge from the interaction between persistent internal body models and the altered sensory signals available after amputation, making PLS a valuable model for studying the construction and maintenance of body representations (Makin et al., 2013; Makin & Bensmaia, 2017).

text.text: Prosthetic devices are a central component of rehabilitation after limb loss.
They are primarily designed to restore or support lost motor functions and thereby improve autonomy in daily life (Horgan & MacLachlan, 2004; Murray & Fox, 2002).
text.formatted: They are primarily designed to restore or support lost motor functions and thereby improve autonomy in daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Horgan & MacLachlan, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Murray & Fox, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond functional compensation, prostheses may also shape how persons with an amputation experience their changed body, including body image, perceived bodily completeness, and adaptation mechanisms to the functional and social consequences of limb loss (Gozaydinoglu et al., 2019; Horgan & MacLachlan, 2004; Murray & Fox, 2002).

text.text: However, functional use of a prosthesis does not necessarily imply bodily integration, as the device may support action while still being represented as an external object rather than as part of the body.
In persons with an amputation and PLS, prosthesis embodiment may depend on how the prosthesis relates to the phantom limb.

Qualitative studies indicate that phantom sensations can either facilitate or interfere with prosthesis use: some describe the phantom and prosthesis as merging, whereas others experience them as spatially or functionally incompatible (Bouffard et al., 2012; Giummarra et al., 2010).

text.text: Consistent with this distinction, recent work suggests that the degree to which the phantom limb is consciously experienced as part of the bodily self (phantom self-consciousness) contributes to prosthesis embodiment only when the phantom and the prosthesis can be perceived as co-located, a phenomenon described as phantom-prosthesis tolerance (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2022).

text.text: Thus, the interaction between the phantom and physical objects may be critical to understanding whether an artificial limb is incorporated into the bodily self or remains an external tool.
A particularly informative case is the interaction between the phantom limb and ordinary physical obstacles.

In obstacle tolerance (OBT), the phantom remains present even when its perceived position overlaps with a solid object, for example, when the residual limb is placed against a wall, and the phantom is felt as extending into or through it (Jalavisto, 1950; Saetta et al., 2018).

text.text: In obstacle shunning (OBS), by contrast, the phantom retracts, fades, or disappears when such overlap would occur.

The phantom therefore appears to respect the physical constraint that two solid objects cannot occupy the same space, often referred to as the law of impenetrability (E. D. Chen, 2020; Saetta et al., 2018).

text.text: These phenomena show that a limb with no physical mass can nevertheless be constrained by physical matter at the level of bodily experience.
As such, OBS and OBT provide a useful model for investigating how bodily representations interact with external space when direct sensory input from the limb is no longer available.

text.text: OBS and OBT are associated with distinct perceptual biases when a limb appears to move through or around an obstacle, suggesting that phantomobject relations influence visuomotor representations.
Whether these differences are also expressed during goal-directed interaction with real objects remains unclear.
Addressing this question would help determine whether the previously reported perceptual differences extend to action and visual monitoring of obstacles.
In doing so, it would clarify the relationship between phantom limb experience and body representations used during action after amputation.
Visual attention provides a direct behavioural window into this question.
During natural action, gaze is directed toward information that supports movement planning, online control, and obstacle avoidance (Hayhoe & Ballard, 2005; Johansson et al., 2001; Ross et al., 2015).
text.formatted: During natural action, gaze is directed toward information that supports movement planning, online control, and obstacle avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hayhoe & Ballard, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Johansson et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Ross et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Gaze toward an obstacle can therefore indicate how behaviourally relevant that obstacle is for the acting body.
This is especially relevant in persons with an amputation because visual information can strongly influence phantom limb perception.

Mirror visual feedback, a therapeutic approach that uses the reflection of the intact limb to create the visual illusion of the missing limb, and related visual manipulations can alter phantom posture, movement, and pain, showing that visual signals remain shaping body representation even in the absence of afferent input from the missing limb (Hunter, 2003; V. S. Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, 1996).

text.text: In the present study, we investigated whether the distinction between OBS and OBT is reflected in visual attention during obstacle avoidance.
Participants completed a limb repositioning task in which they physically executed or imagined movements from one side of a real obstacle to the other.
This allowed us to test whether phantom-object relations previously identified in perceptual paradigms are also expressed during goaldirected interaction with physical objects.
We focused on obstacle-directed gaze as an implicit marker of the obstacle's behavioural relevance for the perceived body.

We further examined trial duration and visual attention shifts between the obstacle and the limb or surrounding environment, because these measures provide complementary information about task-related demands and the dynamic allocation of attention during obstacle avoidance.

We hypothesised that, if OBS reflects a conflict between the perceived phantom limb and physical object boundaries, individuals with OBS should allocate more visual attention to the obstacle when the affected limb is involved.
They should also show longer trial durations if dealing with this conflict increases cognitive or sensorimotor demands.

In contrast, if OBT reflects tolerance of phantom-object overlap, obstacle-directed gaze should be reduced or less strongly modulated by the affected limb due to the absence of a conflict between the perceived phantom limb and physical object boundaries.

text.text: In this exercise, the obstacle consisted of a wooden box with dimensions 26 × 16.5 × 31.7 cm (Height × Width × Length), and the start and end marks for the repositioning of the limb were placed 13cm from each side of the obstacle.

The repositioning task was performed in two conditions: Motor Execution (by physically moving the limb from the start to the end position) and Motor Imagery (by mentally performing the movement without moving the physical limb).
In this study, we analysed the gaze behaviour data from these tasks, leaving the accelerometer data for a future analysis.
Gaze behaviour was recorded in this dataset by the Tobii Glasses 2 system (Tobii Pro Glasses 2, 2016), with a sampling rate of 100 Hz, with accuracy and precision of 0.5° and 0.3° RMS.
World video was also acquired with a 1920 by 1080-pixel resolution at 25 frames per second, with a horizontal and vertical field of view of approximately 82° and 52°.
Further information about the validation of the accuracy of the eye-tracking system can be found in (Cognolato et al., 2020).

To interpret when the gaze of the participants was over the obstacle when performing the repositioning task, two neural network models for object detection in images were used: one for the able-bodied participants and another for the participants with an amputation.

This was done to increase the precision of the Region of Interest (ROI) segmentation, as data from able-bodied participants were collected in a laboratory environment, while data from participants with an amputation were collected in a clinical environment with differences in background, colour, and illumination.

The segmentation was performed in both cases with a Faster R-CNN model (Ren et al., 2016), which was retrained in Python 3.8 (Python 3.8.0, 2019) and PyTorch (PyTorch, 2024) with 870 manually segmented video frames from all the able-bodied participants for their segmentation model, and 450 manually segmented frames from all the clinical population videos for the other model.

text.text: Each model outputted the X and Y positions of the top-left and bottom-right corners of the square ROI segmenting the obstacle (four values in total).

Since the sampling rate of the world camera (25 fps) was four times slower than the sampling rate for the eye camera (100 Hz), the position of the ROI was linearly interpolated between frames for a more accurate estimation of the position of the region of interest with respect to the participants' gaze.

text.text: Since Dwell times have been related to increases in cognitive and affective processing load (Aleya et al., 2022; Paletta et al., 2014; Walter & Bex, 2021), the Dwell-time Ratio inside the ROI and Trial Duration metrics were extracted for each trial, as well as the number of Attentional Shifts crossing the ROI limits.

text.text: Dwell-time Ratio and Trial Duration were chosen instead of raw Dwell time to disentangle whether the influence on gaze behaviour was due to the diversion of visual attention towards the obstacle or to the time taken to perform the task, rather than to their combination.

text.text: Differences among experimental Conditions were assessed using posterior contrasts of estimated marginal means from Bayesian mixed-effects models.

Marginal means were computed at the population level by excluding random effects derived from predictions for the Dwell-time Ratio and Trial Duration models, yielding populationaverage estimates rather than subject-specific predictions.
For nonlinear hurdle models for the Attention Shifts, marginal means were computed by integrating over participantlevel random effects to obtain population-averaged estimates.
Pairwise contrasts were evaluated on the latent scale, and the strength of evidence was quantified using 95% highest-density intervals and the probability of direction.
For the analysis of the dependent variables of the ratio of Dwell time and trial duration, the following formula was used:

Where Dependent variable would correspond to Dwell Time Ratio inside the ROI or Trial Duration; Condition would be each of the possible combinations between populations (Control, OBS, and OBT) and the limb used to perform the task (Intact or Affected); ID would correspond to the participant identifier and was used to take into account individual differences in the intercept.
The decision to use Condition was made to avoid an imbalance in the model caused by the lack of amputated limbs in the control population.
The same formulas and model parameters were used for both modalities, Motor Execution and Motor Imagery.
The Dwell Time Ratio inside the region of interest (ROI) was analysed using a Bayesian generalised linear mixed-effects model with a Gaussian likelihood and a logit link.

Because the logit transformation is undefined for proportions equal to 0 or 1, Dwelltime Ratios were first adjusted using a standard zero-one rescaling procedure to ensure all values fell strictly within the open interval (0, 1).
Bayesian estimation was implemented in brms using weakly informative Normal priors: Normal (0,1) for the fixed effects and variance parameters.
Four Markov chains were run for 6,000 iterations each (1,500 warm-up), using adapt_delta = 0.99 and max_treedepth = 15 to promote stable sampling.
Convergence was assessed via R-hat statistics, effective sample sizes, and visual inspection of chain mixing.
Inference was based on posterior summaries and 95% highest-density intervals (HDIs).
Estimated marginal means were backtransformed to the original time scale for interpretation and graphical reporting.

Trial Duration was measured in seconds and analysed using a Bayesian generalised linear mixed-effects model with a lognormal likelihood, which is appropriate for strictly positive and positively skewed latency-like outcomes.
Models were fitted using the brms package.

We specified weakly informative Normal priors: a Normal(2, 1) prior on the intercept on the log scale, Normal(0, 1) priors on fixed effects, and a half-Normal(0, 1) prior on the standard deviation of the random intercepts. e ran four Markov chains for 6,000 iterations each (1,500 warm-up) with max_treedepth = 15 and adapt_delta = 0.99 to ensure exploration of the posterior.
Convergence was assessed using R-hat, effective sample sizes, and visual inspection of chain traces.
Inference was based on posterior summaries and 95% highest density intervals (HDIs).
Estimated marginal means were back-transformed to the original scale for interpretation and graphical reporting.
For the analysis of Attention Shifts, the number of saccades crossing the ROI boundary was modelled using a Bayesian hurdle Gaussian mixed-effects model.

Because the empirical distribution showed a substantial point mass at zero and a continuous positive tail, a two-part hurdle formulation was adopted, in which the probability of producing zero saccades or attentional shifts and the distribution of non-zero values are estimated separately (e.g., following the approach in (Moffat & Cross, 2024)).

text.text: To stabilise model fitting and maximise the understanding of the distribution of both value clusters, saccade counts were pre-processed by applying a threshold of 3 saccades, as this value was where the number of Attention Shifts presented the lowest density between both clusters across all the values acquired in the combined data pool of Motor Execution and Motor Imagery tasks.
According to this threshold, values ≤ 3 were recorded as zero, whereas values > 3 retained their observed magnitude.

text.text: The model decomposed the response into two components: a Bernoulli process estimating the probability of a zero outcome (hurdle probability, hu parameter), and a Gaussian distribution for strictly positive saccade counts.
The linear predictor for both components included Condition as a fixed effect, where Condition reflects the combination of population group (Control, OBS, or OBT) and limb used (Intact or Affected).
Participant identity (ID) was included as a random intercept term (1|ID) to account for repeated observations within individuals.

The model formula in brms notation was: 𝐴𝑡𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑆ℎ𝑖𝑓𝑡𝑠 across ROI boundary ∼ Condition+(1|𝐼𝐷), ℎ𝑢 ∼ Condition Bayesian inference was done using brms with weakly informative priors (Normal(6, 1) for the Gaussian intercept; Cauchy(0, 1) for the hurdle intercept; Normal(0, 1) for all regression coefficients; and Normal(0, 1) for random-effects standard deviations).
Four Markov chains were run for 6,000 iterations each (1,500 warm-up), with adapt_delta = 0.99 and max_treedepth = 15 to ensure robust sampling.
Convergence was assessed using R-hat statistics, bulk and tail effective sample sizes, and visual inspection of chain mixing.
Posterior means and 95% highest-density intervals (HDIs) were used for inference.
The same model structure and priors were applied to both Motor Execution and Motor Imagery conditions.

For the study of relationships between demographic data, PLS assessment metrics, and prosthetic use habits, a Bayesian Linear Mixed Model was used for each metric of interest: the proportion of Dwell time inside the ROI, Trial Duration, and Saccades across the ROI boundary.
Similar formulas were used for the models stated above for each metric, with the substitution of the Condition factor by the formula Population * Metric of interest.
Where the Population would be OBT or OBS, and the Metric of Interest would be the predictor of interest from the demographic, PLS assessment, or prosthetic use data.
Additionally, these models were only fitted with data concerning the affected limb.

text.text: Bayesian general mixed-model analyses of trial duration revealed, during the Motor Execution task, strong evidence for longer times in OBS participants using either limb compared with Controls using the intact limb (OBS_Intact: pd = 0.99, Estimate = -0.42, 95% HDI [-0.77, -0.09]; OBS_Affected: pd = 1, Estimate = -0.58, [-0.91, -0.24]).

During the Motor Imagery task, the models similarly indicated strong evidence that OBS participants took longer times compared with Controls using the intact limb (OBS_Intact: pd = 0.99, Estimate = -0.45, 95% HDI [-0.83, -0.08]; OBS_Amputated: pd = 0.99, Estimate = -0.48, [-0.86, -0.11]).
Strong evidence of longer times was found for participants for the affected limb compared with the intact limb across OBT (pd = 1, Estimate = 0.1, [0.06, 0.15]).

Additionally, strong evidence for higher probability of 3 or less Attention Shifts of OBT participants using the affected limb compared with Controls (pd = 1.00, Estimate = -27.79, 95% HDI [-445.18, -0.87]), and with OBS participants with the affected limb ( pd ≈ 1.00, Estimate = -27.46, 95% HDI [-445.03, -0.53]).

text.text: Several factors were analysed to explore the relationship between demographics, prosthetic use, PLS, and the metrics Dwell-time Ratio, Trial Duration, and Attention Shifts during the limb repositioning task.

Due to the more exploratory nature of this part of the analysis, only findings concerning the metric of interest and its possible interaction are discussed in this section when strong evidence and certainty of their effect were present.

No measurement showed strong evidence of an effect on the Dwell-time Ratio.

Neither demographic variables (age, gender, years since amputation), prosthesis-use variables, nor phantom limb sensation measures demonstrated credible effects or interactions with population for the Dwell-time Ratio spent inside the ROI.
Across both populations, there was strong evidence that daily prosthesis use was associated with Trial Duration.

Specifically, greater daily hours wearing a bodypowered (pd = 0.98, Estimate = -0.22, 95% HDI [-0.44, -0.00]) or a myoelectric open/close (pd = 0.99, Estimate = -0.10, 95% HDI [-0.18, -0.03]) prosthesis were associated with lower Trial Durations.

In addition, there was strong evidence of an interaction between gender and population, indicating that female participants showed longer Trial Durations when presenting OBS compared to OBT (pd = 0.99, Estimate = -1.08, 95% HDI [-1.84, -0.20]).

There was strong evidence that years since amputation was associated with a higher probability of making three or fewer Attention Shifts (pd = 0.99, Estimate = 0.14, 95% HDI [0.05, 0.25]), an effect bigger in participants suffering from OBS rather than OBT (pd = 1.00, Estimate = -0.41, 95% HDI [-0.61, -0.21]).
Strong evidence of an effect was also observed for daily prosthesis use, including cosmetic, body-powered, and myoelectric prostheses.

Increased daily use of a cosmetic prosthesis was associated with a lower probability of performing three or fewer Attention Shifts (pd = 1.00, Estimate = -0.40, 95% HDI [-0.56, -0.24]), with a corresponding interaction effect showing a stronger effect in the OBT compared with the OBS population (pd = 0.98, Estimate = -0.17, 95% HDI [-0.65, -0.00]).

Similarly, increased daily use of a myoelectric open/close prosthesis was associated with a lower probability of performing three or fewer Attention Shifts (pd = 0.98, Estimate = -0.40, 95% HDI [-0.33, -0.02]), with an interaction effect showing a stronger effect in the OBS compared with the OBT population (pd = 1.00, Estimate = 0.45, 95% HDI [0.16, 0.78]).

Lastly, increased daily use of a body-powered prosthesis was associated with a higher probability of performing three or fewer Attention Shifts (pd = 0.98, Estimate = 4.70, 95% HDI [0.54, 45.66]), with an interaction effect showing a stronger effect in the OBT compared with the OBS population (pd = 1.00, Estimate = 9.61, 95% HDI [1.11, 91.52]).

Regarding phantom limb phenomenology, there was strong evidence that a greater frequency of the feeling that the phantom limb can be moved intentionally was associated with a lower probability of performing three or fewer Attention Shifts (pd = 0.99, Estimate = -0.53, 95% HDI [-0.96, -0.09]).

Additionally, there was strong evidence that the Intensity of the feeling that the phantom limb can be moved intentionally was associated with a lower probability of performing three or fewer Attention Shifts on the OBT compared to the OBS population (pd = 1.00, Estimate = -6.02, 95% HDI [-85.00, -0.26]).

Strong evidence of an interaction effect was found for the intensity of phantom limb movement conjointly with the intact limb with a higher probability of performing three or fewer Attention Shifts in the OBT compared with the OBS population (pd = 1.00, Estimate = 6.32, 95% HDI [0.03, 80.04]).

Finally, there was strong evidence of an interaction between gender and population, indicating that male participants showed a higher probability of performing three or fewer attention shifts when exhibiting OBT behaviour in comparison to OBS (pd = 1.00, E = 0.99, HDI [0.24, 1.69]).

Regarding the number of Attention Shifts performed by the participants (given more than three), there was strong evidence for fewer Attention Shifts with increasing years since amputation (pd = 0.99, Estimate = -0.54, 95% HDI [-0.91, -0.14]).

In addition, daily hours wearing a cosmetic prosthesis showed strong evidence of a positive association with the number of Attention Shifts performed (pd = 1.00, Estimate = 0.92, 95% HDI [0.47, 1.37]).

The present study examined the extent to which obstacle shunning (OBS) and obstacle tolerance (OBT), two distinct ways in which a phantom limb relates to physical matter, are reflected in visual attention and task performance near a real obstacle.
The clearest pattern emerged during motor execution.

Participants with OBT spent a smaller proportion of the trial looking at the obstacle with the affected than with the intact limb and were more likely to complete affected-limb trials with three or fewer attention shifts.
Participants with OBS, in contrast, took longer than controls to complete the task, with this delay being also present during motor imagery.
Thus, the gaze effect was expressed mainly as reduced obstacle monitoring in OBT rather than as a direct increase in OBS.
Together, the findings indicate that phantom-object relations extend beyond subjective reports and illusory perception to the visual and temporal organisation of goal-directed behaviour.

These findings contribute to the understanding of body representation after amputation, highlighting the relevance of both phantom limb experience and its relationship with physical objects during action, as reflected in visual attention and task performance.
The two gaze measures in OBT converge on a pattern of reduced obstacle monitoring during affected-limb movements.

This distinction concerned both the proportion of time spent looking at the obstacle and the probability that a trial remained within the lowshift range, as when more than three attention shifts occurred, there was no clear evidence that their number differed across conditions.

During natural action, gaze is closely coupled to the information needed for movement planning and online control (Hayhoe & Ballard, 2005; Johansson et al., 2001), and fixation location can influence the trajectory selected during obstacle avoidance (Ross et al., 2015).

text.text: Against this background, the OBT findings suggest that the obstacle carries less information that needs to be repeatedly sampled when phantom-object overlap is tolerated.
This does not imply a weaker phantom representation.
Rather, the phantom-object relation may be sufficiently stable that the obstacle boundary creates less uncertainty about the phantom's position or continuity.
A shorter residual limb may also reduce physical collision risk and contribute to this pattern.
The longer trial durations in OBS point to a complementary aspect of the same bodyobject relation.

OBS participants were slower than controls with both the intact and affected limbs, while both groups with an amputation were slower with the affected than with the intact limb during motor execution.
Longer movement times are generally associated with greater sensorimotor or attentional demands (Mahboobin et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Longer movement times are generally associated with greater sensorimotor or attentional demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Mahboobin et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In OBS, however, a nearby object has an additional consequence, as overlap can cause the phantom to retract, fade, or disappear.
Acting near an obstacle may therefore require the intended movement to be reconciled with a body representation whose spatial continuity can change in the presence of physical matter.
The fact that slowing in OBS was also evident for the intact limb suggests that this may become a broader action strategy rather than a response confined to the phantom side.
Trial duration cannot identify the underlying mechanism on its own, but together with the gaze findings, it points to different ways of managing body-object constraints in OBS and OBT.
The conceptual importance of these findings becomes clearer when they are considered alongside previous apparent-motion work.
In apparent-motion paradigms, two images of a limb presented on opposite sides of an obstacle create the impression that the limb has moved between them.

At short stimulus intervals, observers tend to perceive the shorter path of the limb moving through the obstacle; with more time, prior knowledge about the body and solid objects increasingly favours a physically plausible path around it (Shiffrar & Freyd, 1990; Stevens et al., 2000). Saetta et al. (2018) reproduced this general effect in participants with an amputation and controls but also found opposite biases within the group with an amputation.

(2018)</ref> reproduced this general effect in participants with an amputation and controls but also found opposite biases within the group with an amputation.

text.text: OBS was associated with more throughobject percepts, whereas OBT was associated with more around-object percepts.
At first sight, the OBT result may seem paradoxical because these participants consciously tolerate phantom-object overlap.

The proposed explanation was that, precisely because the phantom remains spatially present when an object occupies the same location, its represented volume continues to behave as body-related space and solidity constraints remain relevant.
In OBS, by contrast, overlap can be resolved by retraction or disappearance of the phantom, reducing the perceptual conflict created by a throughobject trajectory.
The present task preserved the same basic spatial configuration but moved from an ambiguous visual illusion to action around a real obstacle.

The findings are therefore complementary rather than contradictory, since apparent motion concerns which path is perceived, whereas gaze reflects how much visual monitoring is required while an action is organised.
A stable phantom representation, as in OBT, may strongly constrain perceived trajectories while requiring less repeated checking of an obstacle that does not disrupt phantom continuity.
One possible mechanism linking these findings is that OBS and OBT differ in how visual information is weighted relative to the persistent representation of the missing limb.

Phantom awareness is not insulated from external sensory input. Hunter (2003) showed that normal vision could suppress the phantom component of touch-evoked dual percepts, whereas a mirror illusion transiently enhanced spontaneous phantom awareness in several participants with an amputation.

text.text: Mirror visual feedback can also evoke sensations of phantom movement (V. S. Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, 1996).

text.text: Neuroprosthetic studies extend the same principle, indicating that kinesthetic feedback can be integrated within minutes to improve prosthetic movement control and increase agency (Marasco et al., 2018), while temporally congruent visual and neural tactile feedback can increase prosthesis embodiment and reduce distorted phantom shortening (Rognini et al., 2019).

text.text: Together, these findings show that post-amputation body representation remains responsive to congruent visual and multisensory information.

In OBS, an object boundary may therefore require more processing because it can alter the experienced phantom, while in OBT the same boundary may require less repeated verification because overlap leaves the phantom intact.

The present data do not show that gaze itself changes phantom perception, but they are consistent with differences in the behavioural relevance assigned to visual information about physical boundaries.

There was no strong evidence of differences in obstacle dwell-time ratio during imagery, and the probability of making three or fewer attention shifts depended on both group and the limb being imagined.

This divergence is consistent with previous evidence that phantom motor execution and motor imagery are distinct processes rather than interchangeable forms of the same representation. Raffin et al. (2012) showed that persons with an amputation could both execute and imagine phantom movements, with execution accompanied by stump muscle activity and slower phantom than intact-limb movements, whereas imagined movements showed comparable timing for the two sides.

(2012)</ref> showed that persons with an amputation could both execute and imagine phantom movements, with execution accompanied by stump muscle activity and slower phantom than intact-limb movements, whereas imagined movements showed comparable timing for the two sides.

text.text: The two conditions also recruited partially overlapping but dissociable neural networks, with execution engaging sensorimotor regions more strongly and imagery relying relatively more on parietal and occipital regions.
In the present task, executed movement required online control of an evolving body-object relation, whereas imagery required the trajectory to be internally simulated without an actual collision.
Phantom-object relations may therefore influence visual attention differently depending on whether an action is being physically controlled or mentally simulated.
The exploratory analyses suggest that obstacle monitoring may also relate to the history and motor qualities of the phantom.
Longer time since amputation was associated with a greater probability of trials with three or fewer attention shifts and, among trials above this threshold, with fewer shifts overall.

Earlier observations suggested that obstacle shunning experiences become less frequent with increasing age and time since amputation, although (Jalavisto, 1950) examined much shorter and more coarsely defined post-amputation intervals (after amputation and six months after, instead of years as in our sample).

text.text: Additionally, more frequent sensations of being able to move the phantom intentionally were associated with a higher probability of making more attention shifts.
Greater intensity of these sensations showed the same association in OBT participants.

Voluntary phantom movements have been associated with a smaller discrepancy between the phantom and the prosthesis and greater prosthesis embodiment (Giummarra et al., 2010), potentially favouring behaviours associated with intact limbs.
text.formatted: Voluntary phantom movements have been associated with a smaller discrepancy between the phantom and the prosthesis and greater prosthesis embodiment <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Giummarra et al., 2010)</ref>, potentially favouring behaviours associated with intact limbs.

text.text: Stronger sensations of the phantom moving conjointly with the intact limb were associated with a greater probability of making fewer attention shifts in OBT participants.

This pattern may relate to shared neural pathways involved in phantom and intact-limb motor execution, including the primary motor cortex (M1), primary somatosensory cortex (S1), and cerebellum (Anderson & Lenz, 2011; Raffin et al., 2012).

text.text: These regions and sensorimotor internal models contribute to motor planning, particularly during complex coordinated movements (H. Chen et al., 2006; Crammond, 1997; Wolpert & Ghahramani, 2000).

text.text: If conjoint phantom-intact limb movements depend on shared sensorimotor models, participants reporting stronger conjoint movements may represent the phantom more similarly to the intact limb.

These findings are compatible with the broader view that phantom limbs retain dynamic postural and motor properties and can remain incorporated into ongoing sensorimotor representations (Giummarra et al., 2010; Raffin et al., 2012).

text.text: They raise the possibility that visual monitoring changes with the stability or controllability of the phantom, but the present cross-sectional data cannot establish adaptation over time.
This possibility could be tested by measuring phantom position and perceived movement control alongside gaze across repeated sessions.
This would allow examination of whether changes in phantom controllability and stability are accompanied by changes in visual attention during obstacle monitoring.
Prosthesis use provides a further connection between the present findings and experience-dependent body representation.

Greater daily use of body-powered and myoelectric prostheses was associated with shorter trial durations, while associations between prosthesis use and attention shifts differed across device types and did not form a single consistent pattern.
The device-specific effects should therefore remain exploratory.

The broader literature nevertheless shows that prosthetic experience can reshape both the represented body and the space surrounding it. Canzoneri et al. (2013) found that, without a prosthesis, perceived arm length and peripersonal-space boundaries shifted towards the stump; wearing the prosthesis increased perceived limb extent and expanded peripersonal space to include the prosthetic hand.

(2013)</ref> found that, without a prosthesis, perceived arm length and peripersonal-space boundaries shifted towards the stump; wearing the prosthesis increased perceived limb extent and expanded peripersonal space to include the prosthetic hand.

text.text: Bekrater-Bodmann (2022) further showed that perceived phantom-prosthesis co-location mediated the relationship between phantom self-consciousness and prosthesis embodiment.

These results converge on a common principle: embodiment depends not only on the vividness of a phantom, but also on whether the phantom can be spatially reconciled with physical objects and artificial limbs.
OBS and OBT may capture one aspect of this spatial compatibility.

The present gaze effects could therefore provide a behavioural index of how the perceived body is organised relative to nearby physical matter, although neither peripersonal space nor prosthesis embodiment was measured directly here.
Several limitations should also be considered when interpreting these results.

The sample included 15 participants with an amputation, divided into seven OBS and eight OBT participants, and the prosthesis subgroups were smaller still, with gender-related findings being particularly difficult to interpret because only two participants with amputation were women.
Some attention-shift estimates had very wide credible intervals, and the threshold of three shifts was derived from the observed distribution.
OBS and OBT were treated categorically, although phantom-object and phantomprosthesis relations may be better represented dimensionally (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2022).
text.formatted: OBS and OBT were treated categorically, although phantom-object and phantomprosthesis relations may be better represented dimensionally <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bekrater-Bodmann, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Gaze and trial duration are indirect measures and cannot determine whether a fixation reflects anticipatory planning, online control, conflict monitoring, or postmovement checking.
The study also lacked an obstacle-free comparison, so longer trial durations cannot be attributed specifically to phantom-object conflict.

Residual-limb geometry may contribute to collision risk, and control and participants with amputation recordings were obtained in different environments, requiring separate obstaclesegmentation models.
Finally, motor execution and imagery were analysed separately rather than within a direct task comparison.

Future studies could combine mobile eye tracking with movement kinematics, electromyography, and trial-by-trial measures of phantom position to examine how obstacle monitoring relates to movement execution and the experienced spatial configuration of the phantom.

Testing apparent-motion perception and real obstacle avoidance in the same participants would be particularly informative because it would determine whether illusion-based OBS/OBT biases predict the visual strategies used around real objects.

Standardised recording conditions and dimensional measures of phantom-object compatibility would improve precision, while longitudinal studies incorporating validated measures of prosthesis embodiment could establish whether phantom-object relations, gaze behaviour, and prosthesis integration change together over time.
Taken together, the main findings extend OBS and OBT from phenomenology and visual illusion to action-related visuospatial processing.

In OBT, affected-limb movements were accompanied by less obstacle-directed gaze and a greater probability of fewer attention shifts, consistent with reduced need to monitor a boundary that does not disrupt phantom continuity.
In OBS, longer task durations are consistent with greater demands when action occurs near a boundary that can alter the experienced phantom.
The distinction is not expressed as a simple opposition across every measure or task.
Instead, phantom-object phenomenology appears to interact with the specific demands of visual monitoring, movement control, and motor simulation.
This provides a more behaviourally-grounded account of how a physically absent limb can continue to structure interactions with the external world.
